units.title: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

cards.q: State what the notation $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means in words.
cards.a: As x takes values closer and closer to a from both sides (without ever equaling a), the outputs f(x) get arbitrarily close to the single number L.
cards.n: The limit describes behavior NEAR a, never AT a; f(a) may be undefined or a different value entirely.

cards.q: Explain the three ways a two-sided limit can fail to exist.
cards.a: (1) The left- and right-hand limits exist but disagree. (2) The function oscillates without settling, as with sin(1/x) at 0. (3) The values grow without bound.
cards.n: Writing 'the limit equals ∞' is a description of unbounded behavior; formally the limit does not exist.

cards.q: Define the two one-sided limits and give their notation.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x)$ uses only inputs x < a (approach from the left). $\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x)$ uses only inputs x > a (approach from the right).

cards.q: State the relationship between the one-sided limits and the two-sided limit.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ exactly when $\lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = L$. Both one-sided limits must exist AND agree.
cards.n: This is the tool for piecewise functions: always evaluate each side with its own formula.

cards.q: State the limit laws for sums, constant multiples, products, and quotients.
cards.a: If $\lim_{x \to a} f$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g$ both exist: lim(f ± g) = lim f ± lim g; lim(cf) = c·lim f; lim(fg) = (lim f)(lim g); and lim(f/g) = (lim f)/(lim g) provided lim g ≠ 0.
cards.n: Every law requires the individual limits to exist first; splitting a limit that does not exist is a classic error.

cards.q: Explain when direct substitution is guaranteed to produce a limit.
cards.a: When f is continuous at a. Polynomials are continuous everywhere; rational, root, trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions are continuous at every point of their domain, so there $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.

cards.q: Describe the algebraic move for a limit of a rational expression that gives the form 0/0.
cards.a: Factor the numerator and the denominator, cancel the common factor that produces the zero, then substitute into the simplified expression.
cards.n: Cancelling is legal because x ≠ a throughout the limit process; the simplified function agrees with the original except at a.

cards.q: Describe the algebraic move for a 0/0 limit containing a square root.
cards.a: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the radical expression, use (√A - √B)(√A + √B) = A - B to clear the root, cancel the offending factor, then substitute.

cards.q: Describe how to evaluate a 0/0 limit built from a complex (stacked) fraction.
cards.a: Multiply the numerator and denominator of the big fraction by the common denominator of the small fractions to clear them, simplify, cancel, then substitute.

cards.q: State the special trigonometric limit involving sine of x over x.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$
cards.n: The argument must match top and bottom and go to 0: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{x} = 3$.

cards.q: State the special trigonometric limit involving 1 minus cosine of x over x.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x} = 0$
cards.n: Do not confuse it with $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}$, which has a squared denominator.

cards.q: State the Squeeze Theorem, including its hypotheses.
cards.a: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) for all x in an open interval containing a (except possibly at a), and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$.
cards.n: The two outer limits must be EQUAL; the classic use is bounding a bounded-times-small product such as x² sin(1/x).

cards.q: Describe how to set up a squeeze for a function like f(x) = x² sin(1/x) near x = 0.
cards.a: Start from the bound -1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, multiply through by the nonnegative factor x² to get -x² ≤ f(x) ≤ x², and note both outer limits are 0.
cards.n: Multiplying an inequality by a negative quantity reverses it, so justify that the multiplier is nonnegative.

cards.q: Contrast removable, jump, and infinite discontinuity.
cards.a: Removable: the two-sided limit exists but f(a) is undefined or unequal to it (a hole). Jump: both one-sided limits exist but differ. Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is +∞ or -∞, giving a vertical asymptote.
cards.n: Only the removable kind can be repaired by redefining a single value.

cards.q: State the three conditions required for f to be continuous at x = a.
cards.a: (1) f(a) is defined. (2) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists. (3) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
cards.n: On free response, name all three conditions explicitly when asked to justify continuity at a point.

cards.q: Explain what it means for f to be continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
cards.a: f is continuous at every interior point of (a, b), and one-sided continuous at the ends: $\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = f(a)$ and $\lim_{x \to b^{-}} f(x) = f(b)$.

cards.q: Describe how to choose a constant that makes a piecewise function continuous at its break point x = c.
cards.a: Set the left-hand piece evaluated at c equal to the right-hand piece evaluated at c, and equal to the defined value f(c); solve the resulting equation for the unknown constant.

cards.q: Explain how to remove a removable discontinuity at x = a.
cards.a: Redefine f(a) to be $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$. This works only when that limit exists as a finite number, so jump and infinite discontinuities can never be removed.

cards.q: State the connection between infinite limits and vertical asymptotes.
cards.a: The line x = a is a vertical asymptote of f exactly when at least one one-sided limit at a is +∞ or -∞. For a rational function this happens where the denominator is 0 and the numerator is not.
cards.n: If a factor cancels completely, the graph has a hole there instead of an asymptote.

cards.q: Predict the sign of a rational function on each side of a vertical asymptote.
cards.a: Test a value just left and just right of a and track the sign of every factor. A zero factor of odd multiplicity gives opposite infinite signs on the two sides; even multiplicity gives the same sign on both sides.

cards.q: Decide the horizontal asymptote of a rational function from the degrees of its numerator and denominator.
cards.a: Numerator degree < denominator degree: y = 0. Degrees equal: y = ratio of the leading coefficients. Numerator degree greater: no horizontal asymptote (there is a slant or polynomial asymptote instead).
cards.n: A graph may cross its horizontal asymptote; the asymptote only describes end behavior.

cards.q: Describe the algebraic technique for evaluating a limit at infinity of a rational expression.
cards.a: Divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the highest power of x appearing in the denominator, then apply $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x^{n}} = 0$ for n > 0.

cards.q: Evaluate the end-behavior limits of e^x, ln x, and arctan x.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to \infty} e^{x} = \infty$ and $\lim_{x \to -\infty} e^{x} = 0$; $\lim_{x \to \infty} \ln x = \infty$ and $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \ln x = -\infty$; $\lim_{x \to \infty} \arctan x = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

cards.q: Explain the sign trap when taking a limit as x approaches negative infinity of an expression with a square root.
cards.a: For x < 0, $\sqrt{x^{2}} = -x$, not x. Pulling x out of a radical without the absolute value loses a minus sign and flips the sign of the horizontal asymptote.
cards.n: Rational functions with a radical often have TWO different horizontal asymptotes for this reason.

cards.q: State the Intermediate Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and k is any number between f(a) and f(b), then there exists at least one c in the open interval (a, b) with f(c) = k.
cards.n: Continuity on the CLOSED interval is required; drop it and the conclusion can fail.

cards.q: Explain the exact wording needed to justify the existence of a root using the IVT.
cards.a: Say: f is continuous on [a, b] (state why, e.g. it is a polynomial); f(a) < 0 < f(b) (show both computed values); therefore by the Intermediate Value Theorem there is a c in (a, b) with f(c) = 0.
cards.n: Naming continuity and showing the two endpoint values are both scored; the conclusion alone earns nothing.

cards.q: Explain what the Intermediate Value Theorem does NOT guarantee.
cards.a: It gives existence only, not uniqueness — there may be several such c. It does not locate c, and it gives no information at all if f has any discontinuity on [a, b].

cards.q: Explain how to estimate a limit from a table of values, and the caution required.
cards.a: Choose x-values marching toward a from both sides and watch whether the outputs stabilize toward one number. A table can only suggest a limit; it never proves the limit exists.

cards.q: Identify what the graph of f looks like at a removable discontinuity.
cards.a: An open circle at (a, L), where L is the common value of both one-sided limits, with the curve approaching that height from both sides. A separate filled dot may sit elsewhere above or below x = a.

cards.q: Contrast average rate of change and instantaneous rate of change.
cards.a: Average rate of change on [a, b] is the secant slope $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. Instantaneous rate of change at a is the tangent slope f'(a), the limit of secant slopes as the second point approaches a.
cards.n: Average rate needs an interval; instantaneous rate needs a single point.

cards.q: State the limit definition of the derivative in the h form.
cards.a: $f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$, whenever this limit exists.
cards.n: If a question says 'using the definition of the derivative', an answer found with the power rule earns no credit.

cards.q: State the limit definition of the derivative at a point in the x-approaches-a form.
cards.a: $f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}$, whenever this limit exists.

cards.q: Identify the standard notations that all denote the derivative of y = f(x).
cards.a: f'(x), y', $\frac{dy}{dx}$, $\frac{df}{dx}$, and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( f(x) \right)$. At a specific input the value is written f'(a).

cards.q: Identify the function and the point hidden in the limit $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\left( 2+h \right)^{5} - 32}{h}$, then evaluate it.
cards.a: It matches $f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ with $f(x) = x^{5}$ and a = 2. So the limit is $f'(2) = 5 \cdot 2^{4} = 80$.
cards.n: Multiple choice loves this reversal: recognize the difference quotient instead of trying to expand.

cards.q: Describe how to estimate f'(a) from a table of values.
cards.a: Use a difference quotient over the smallest interval in the table that straddles or touches a, ideally symmetric: $\frac{f(b)-f(c)}{b-c}$ with c < a < b. Label the result as an approximation.

cards.q: State the relationship between differentiability and continuity, in both directions.
cards.a: If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a. The converse is FALSE: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there.
cards.n: The contrapositive is the useful form: a discontinuity guarantees non-differentiability.

cards.q: Identify the graphical features at which a function fails to be differentiable.
cards.a: A corner (unequal one-sided derivatives), a cusp (one-sided slopes running to +∞ and -∞), a vertical tangent line, and any point of discontinuity.

cards.q: Explain how to check whether a piecewise function is differentiable at its break point x = c.
cards.a: Two conditions must hold: the two pieces agree in value at c (continuity), and the derivatives of the two pieces agree at c. Set up both equations and solve for the unknown constants.
cards.n: Solving only the derivative equation is the classic mistake; continuity is required first.

cards.q: State the power rule and the rewriting it requires.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( x^{n} \right) = n x^{n-1}$ for every real n. Rewrite radicals and reciprocals as powers first, e.g. $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ and $\frac{1}{x^{3}} = x^{-3}$.

cards.q: State the constant, constant-multiple, and sum/difference derivative rules.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( c \right) = 0$; $\frac{d}{dx} \left( c f(x) \right) = c f'(x)$; $\frac{d}{dx} \left( f(x) \pm g(x) \right) = f'(x) \pm g'(x)$.

cards.q: State the derivatives of sin x and cos x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \sin x \right) = \cos x$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \cos x \right) = -\sin x$.
cards.n: The minus sign belongs to the cosine derivative; these formulas assume x is in radians.

cards.q: State the derivatives of e^x and ln x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( e^{x} \right) = e^{x}$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \ln x \right) = \frac{1}{x}$ for x > 0.

cards.q: State the derivatives of a^x and of log base b of x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( a^{x} \right) = a^{x} \ln a$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \log_{b} x \right) = \frac{1}{x \ln b}$, for a > 0 and b > 0 with b ≠ 1.
cards.n: Both reduce to the familiar e and ln results because ln e = 1.

cards.q: State the product rule.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( f g \right) = f' g + f g'$ — derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second.
cards.n: The derivative of a product is never the product of the derivatives.

cards.q: State the quotient rule.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{f}{g} \right) = \frac{f' g - f g'}{g^{2}}$
cards.n: Order matters: the term with the derivative of the numerator comes first, and the subtraction makes it non-commutative.

cards.q: State the derivatives of tan x and cot x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \tan x \right) = \sec^{2} x$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \cot x \right) = -\csc^{2} x$.

cards.q: State the derivatives of sec x and csc x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \sec x \right) = \sec x \tan x$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \csc x \right) = -\csc x \cot x$.

cards.q: Recall the memory pattern for which trigonometric derivatives carry a minus sign.
cards.a: Every co-function — cos, cot, csc — differentiates to a negative expression. The non-co functions sin, tan, sec differentiate to positive expressions.

cards.q: Explain the geometric meaning of f'(a).
cards.a: It is the slope of the line tangent to the graph of y = f(x) at the point (a, f(a)), obtained as the limiting slope of secant lines through that point.

cards.q: Write the equation of the line tangent to f at x = a.
cards.a: y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a). You need both the function value f(a) for the point and the derivative f'(a) for the slope.
cards.n: Most tangent-line errors come from forgetting to compute f(a) or from evaluating f' at the wrong input.

cards.q: Differentiate $y = \frac{1}{x^{3}} + \sqrt{x}$.
Decide whether to use the quotient rule or to rewrite the expression first.
cards.a: If the denominator is a single term, split the fraction or use a negative exponent instead — it is faster and less error-prone. Save the quotient rule for genuine multi-term denominators.

cards.q: Compute the average rate of change of f on [a, b] and name the line it measures.
cards.a: $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$, which is the slope of the secant line through (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)).

cards.q: State the chain rule.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( f \left( g(x) \right) \right) = f' \left( g(x) \right) \cdot g'(x)$ — the derivative of the outside function evaluated at the unchanged inside, times the derivative of the inside.
cards.n: Forgetting the inner derivative is the single most common differentiation error on the exam.

cards.q: State the chain rule in Leibniz notation.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}$, where y depends on u and u depends on x.

cards.q: Differentiate $y = \sin \left( 3x^{2} \right)$.
cards.a: $y' = \cos \left( 3x^{2} \right) \cdot 6x = 6x \cos \left( 3x^{2} \right)$

cards.q: State the chain-rule versions of the derivatives of e^u, ln u, and sin u.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( e^{u} \right) = e^{u} u'$; $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \ln u \right) = \frac{u'}{u}$; $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \sin u \right) = u' \cos u$, where u is a differentiable function of x.

cards.q: Explain how to differentiate a triple composition.
cards.a: Peel one layer at a time from the outside in, multiplying by the derivative of each successive layer evaluated at everything still inside it. Nothing inside a layer changes until you reach that layer.

cards.q: Explain the classic chain-rule error with a power of a trigonometric function.
cards.a: $\sin^{2} x$ means $\left( \sin x \right)^{2}$, so the power rule gives $2 \sin x$ times the derivative of the inside: the answer is $2 \sin x \cos x$, not $2 \sin x$.

cards.q: Explain the procedure for implicit differentiation.
cards.a: Differentiate both sides with respect to x, attaching $\frac{dy}{dx}$ by the chain rule every time you differentiate a y. Then gather all $\frac{dy}{dx}$ terms on one side, factor it out, and divide.
cards.n: Treat y as an unnamed function of x; every y term produces a dy/dx factor.

cards.q: Differentiate x² + y² = 25 implicitly and solve for dy/dx.
cards.a: $2x + 2y \frac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}$.
cards.n: The answer depends on both x and y, which is normal for an implicit relation.

cards.q: Explain how the product rule appears in implicit differentiation of a term like xy.
cards.a: Since both factors depend on x, $\frac{d}{dx} \left( xy \right) = y + x \frac{dy}{dx}$.

cards.q: Describe how to evaluate dy/dx at a specific point on an implicitly defined curve.
cards.a: Substitute BOTH coordinates into the solved expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$. First confirm the point satisfies the original equation, since a point off the curve gives a meaningless slope.

cards.q: Identify where an implicitly defined curve has a vertical tangent line.
cards.a: Where the solved $\frac{dy}{dx}$ has denominator equal to 0 while its numerator is nonzero, at a point that actually lies on the curve.

cards.q: State the formula for the derivative of an inverse function.
cards.a: $\left( f^{-1} \right)'(a) = \frac{1}{f' \left( f^{-1}(a) \right)}$, valid when f is one-to-one and differentiable and $f' \left( f^{-1}(a) \right) \ne 0$.

cards.q: Explain the practical steps for computing the derivative of an inverse function at x = a.
cards.a: Find the number b with f(b) = a, so that $f^{-1}(a) = b$. Compute f'(b). Take the reciprocal. Locating b is usually the hard step and often comes from a table or by inspection.
cards.n: Students commonly compute f'(a) instead of f'(b); the derivative is evaluated at the INPUT of f, not of the inverse.

cards.q: Explain the graphical reason behind the inverse function derivative formula.
cards.a: The graphs of f and its inverse are reflections across the line y = x, so a tangent of slope m at (b, a) on f becomes a tangent of slope 1/m at (a, b) on the inverse.

cards.q: State the derivatives of arcsin x and arccos x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \arcsin x \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$; the derivative of arccos x is $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$.
cards.n: Both require |x| < 1; the pair differs only by a sign.

cards.q: State the derivatives of arctan x and arccot x.
cards.a: $\frac{d}{dx} \left( \arctan x \right) = \frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$; the derivative of arccot x is $-\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$.
cards.n: There is no radical here, and the denominator is never zero, so these are defined for all real x.

cards.q: State the derivatives of arcsec x and arccsc x.
cards.a: arcsec x has derivative $\frac{1}{|x| \sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$; arccsc x has derivative $-\frac{1}{|x| \sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$.
cards.n: The absolute value on x is required, and these need |x| > 1.

cards.q: Recall the pattern that links the six inverse trigonometric derivatives.
cards.a: They form three pairs sharing one expression, with the co-function (arccos, arccot, arccsc) equal to the negative of its partner. The three expressions are $\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$, $\frac{1}{1+x^{2}}$, and $\frac{1}{|x| \sqrt{x^{2}-1}}$.

cards.q: Differentiate y = arctan(u), where u is a differentiable function of x.
cards.a: $y' = \frac{u'}{1+u^{2}}$ — the inverse trig formula with the inside substituted, multiplied by the derivative of the inside.

cards.q: Define higher-order derivatives and give their notation.
cards.a: The second derivative is f'' = (f')', written f''(x), y'', or $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$. The nth derivative is written $f^{(n)}(x)$ or $\frac{d^{n}y}{dx^{n}}$.

cards.q: Explain how to find the second derivative of an implicitly defined relation.
cards.a: Differentiate the solved expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ again with respect to x, using the quotient rule as needed, then substitute the known expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ wherever it appears so the answer is in x and y only.
cards.n: You may also substitute the original equation to simplify; graders accept any equivalent form in x and y.

cards.q: Decide the order in which to apply rules when a function needs several derivative rules.
cards.a: Identify the OUTERMOST structure first: is the whole expression a sum, a product, a quotient, or a composition? Apply that rule, then repeat the question on each remaining piece.
cards.n: Simplifying algebraically before differentiating often removes a rule entirely.

cards.q: Explain how to interpret f'(a) in an applied context, including units.
cards.a: f'(a) is the instantaneous rate of change of f with respect to its input at the value a, measured in units of f per unit of the input variable.
cards.n: Full credit requires the numeric value, a meaning in context, and correct units; missing units is the usual lost point.

cards.q: Write the meaning of C'(50) = 3.2, where C(x) is the cost in dollars of producing x widgets.
cards.a: When 50 widgets have been produced, the cost is increasing at a rate of about 3.2 dollars per widget.

cards.q: Explain how to phrase a NEGATIVE rate of change in an applied answer.
cards.a: State that the quantity is decreasing, and give the magnitude with units: 'the volume is decreasing at 4 liters per minute', rather than 'increasing at -4 liters per minute'.

cards.q: Explain the difference between f(a), f'(a), and f''(a) in an applied sentence.
cards.a: f(a) is the amount present at a. f'(a) is how fast the amount is changing at a. f''(a) is how fast that rate itself is changing. Their units are units, units per time, and units per time squared.

cards.q: Define the relationship among position, velocity, and acceleration for straight-line motion.
cards.a: If s(t) is position, then velocity is v(t) = s'(t) and acceleration is a(t) = v'(t) = s''(t).

cards.q: Contrast velocity and speed.
cards.a: Velocity is signed and carries direction; speed is |v(t)| and is never negative. Speed reports magnitude only.

cards.q: State the rule for when the speed of a particle is increasing.
cards.a: Speed increases exactly when v(t) and a(t) have the SAME sign, and decreases when they have opposite signs — the particle is accelerating in the direction it is already moving.
cards.n: This is asked constantly; 'v and a agree in sign' is the whole justification required.

cards.q: Identify the condition under which a particle changes direction.
cards.a: At a time where v(t) = 0 or v is undefined AND v changes sign there. A velocity that touches zero without changing sign is not a change of direction.

cards.q: Identify what it means for a particle to be at rest, and what it does not imply.
cards.a: At rest at time t means v(t) = 0. It does not mean acceleration is zero: a ball at the top of its flight has v = 0 while a is still the full downward gravitational value.

cards.q: Explain how to find the times when a particle is moving left or downward.
cards.a: Solve the inequality v(t) < 0 on the stated time domain, and report an interval of TIMES, not of positions.

cards.q: Explain how to describe a particle's motion from the graph of v(t).
cards.a: v above the axis means moving right or up; below means moving left or down; a crossing means a change of direction. The slope of the v graph is acceleration, and matching signs of v and its slope mean speeding up.

cards.q: Describe how to answer 'how fast is the quantity changing' in a non-motion applied context.
cards.a: Differentiate the given model with respect to the stated variable, evaluate at the requested input, then report the value with units of the quantity per unit of the input.

cards.q: Describe how to estimate the rate at which a tabulated quantity is changing.
cards.a: Form a difference quotient over the smallest tabulated interval containing the time in question, state the units (for example degrees per minute), and identify the answer explicitly as an approximation.

cards.q: Identify what dV/dt, dr/dt, and dθ/dt each represent.
cards.a: The rates of change with respect to TIME of volume, radius, and angle. Every given or requested quantity in a related rates problem is such a derivative, with units of that quantity per unit time.

cards.q: Explain the standard method for solving a related rates problem.
cards.a: 1) Draw and name variables. 2) Write an equation relating them that is true at all times. 3) Differentiate both sides with respect to t using the chain rule. 4) Substitute the instantaneous values LAST. 5) Solve and give units.

cards.q: Explain why you must not substitute the instantaneous values before differentiating.
cards.a: A quantity that varies with time must remain a variable through the differentiation. Substituting a number early turns a changing quantity into a constant and erases its rate term.
cards.n: Constants given in the problem (a fixed ladder length, a fixed cone ratio) may be substituted early; changing quantities may not.

cards.q: Recall the geometric relationships most often needed in related rates problems.
cards.a: Pythagorean a² + b² = c²; similar triangle proportions; area and volume formulas (circle πr², sphere $\frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3}$, cone $\frac{1}{3} \pi r^{2} h$, cylinder πr²h); and trigonometric ratios for angle-of-elevation problems.

cards.q: Describe the extra step required in a cone problem where both the radius and the height vary.
cards.a: Use similar triangles from the fixed full-cone dimensions to write r as a multiple of h, substitute to express the volume in one variable, and only then differentiate with respect to t.
cards.n: Skipping this step leaves an unknown dr/dt that the problem never gives you.

cards.q: Describe the setup for a ladder sliding down a wall.
cards.a: With x the distance from the wall and y the height on the wall, x² + y² = L² where L is constant, so $2x \frac{dx}{dt} + 2y \frac{dy}{dt} = 0$.
cards.n: The ladder length does not change, so its derivative is 0 — that is why the right side vanishes.

cards.q: Identify the sign conventions for the given rates in a related rates problem.
cards.a: A quantity that is decreasing takes a NEGATIVE rate: a draining tank, a shrinking radius, a falling ladder top. Assign these signs when writing the givens, not after solving.

cards.q: State the linearization of f at x = a and what it is used for.
cards.a: L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a), the tangent line at a, and f(x) ≈ L(x) for x near a.

cards.q: Decide whether a tangent line approximation is an overestimate or an underestimate.
cards.a: If f is concave down near a (f'' < 0), the tangent lies above the curve, so L overestimates. If f is concave up (f'' > 0), the tangent lies below the curve, so L underestimates.

cards.q: Explain the justification language required for an over- or underestimate claim.
cards.a: Cite the sign of the second derivative: 'Since f''(x) < 0 on this interval, f is concave down, so the tangent line lies above the graph and the approximation is an overestimate.'
cards.n: Answering 'overestimate' with no reference to concavity or f'' earns no justification credit.

cards.q: Describe how to use linearization to estimate √4.1.
Define local linearity and connect it to tangent line approximation.
cards.a: A function is locally linear at a if it is differentiable there: zoomed in far enough, its graph is indistinguishable from its tangent line. That is exactly why the tangent line approximates f near a.

cards.q: State L'Hospital's Rule with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f and g are differentiable near a with g'(x) ≠ 0 near a, and $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}$ has the form $\frac{0}{0}$ or $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, then it equals $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$ whenever that limit exists.

cards.q: Identify the indeterminate forms to which L'Hospital's Rule applies directly.
cards.a: Only $\frac{0}{0}$ and $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, where the infinities may be of either sign.
cards.n: You must verify and SAY that the quotient has an indeterminate form before differentiating; that statement is scored.

cards.q: Identify the indeterminate forms that must be rewritten before L'Hospital's Rule can be used.
cards.a: The product form 0 · ∞, the difference form ∞ - ∞, and the exponential forms $1^{\infty}$, $0^{0}$, and $\infty^{0}$. Convert products to quotients, combine differences over a common denominator, and take logarithms of exponential forms.

cards.q: Describe how to handle a limit of the indeterminate form $1^{\infty}$.
cards.a: Set y equal to the expression, take the natural log of both sides to reach a 0 · ∞ or $\frac{0}{0}$ form, apply L'Hospital's Rule to get $\lim_{x \to a} \ln y = L$, then the original limit is e raised to L.
cards.n: Forgetting the final exponentiation and reporting L is the standard trap.

cards.q: Explain the two most common errors when applying L'Hospital's Rule.
cards.a: Using the quotient rule instead of differentiating numerator and denominator SEPARATELY, and applying the rule when the form is not indeterminate (such as 2/0 or 0/5), which produces a wrong answer.

cards.q: Describe what to do when one application of L'Hospital's Rule still yields 0/0.
cards.a: Confirm the new quotient is still indeterminate, simplify it, and apply the rule again. Repeat as needed, simplifying between steps to keep the algebra manageable.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x}$ and state the growth ranking it illustrates.
cards.a: The form is $\frac{\infty}{\infty}$, so it equals $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x} = 0$. Logarithms grow more slowly than positive powers of x, which grow more slowly than exponentials.

cards.q: State the Mean Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] AND differentiable on the open interval (a, b), then there exists at least one c in (a, b) with $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$.
cards.n: Both hypotheses must be stated; continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval are different requirements.

cards.q: Explain the geometric meaning of the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.a: Somewhere strictly inside the interval the tangent line is parallel to the secant line through the endpoints — the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change at least once.

cards.q: Explain how to write an MVT justification that earns full credit.
cards.a: State that f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b) and why; compute the average rate $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$; then conclude 'therefore by the Mean Value Theorem there exists a c in (a, b) with f'(c) equal to that value.'
cards.n: Say 'by the Mean Value Theorem' by name; the hypotheses plus the named theorem are the scored elements.

cards.q: State Rolle's Theorem and relate it to the Mean Value Theorem.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b), then there exists c in (a, b) with f'(c) = 0. It is the MVT in the case where the secant slope is zero.

cards.q: Decide whether the Mean Value Theorem applies to f(x) = |x| on [-1, 2].
cards.a: No. f is continuous on [-1, 2], but it is not differentiable at x = 0, which lies inside the interval, so the differentiability hypothesis fails and no conclusion is guaranteed.

cards.q: State the consequence of the MVT about a function whose derivative is identically zero.
cards.a: If f'(x) = 0 for every x in an interval, then f is constant on that interval. Consequently, if f' = g' on an interval, then f and g differ by a constant there.

cards.q: State the Extreme Value Theorem with its hypotheses.
cards.a: If f is continuous on a closed, bounded interval [a, b], then f attains both an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value at some points of [a, b].
cards.n: Both 'continuous' and 'closed interval' are required; the theorem guarantees existence but not location.

cards.q: Explain why the Extreme Value Theorem can fail on an open interval.
cards.a: Without endpoints, values can be approached but never attained: f(x) = x on (0, 1) has neither a maximum nor a minimum, even though it is continuous.

cards.q: Define a critical point of f.
cards.a: An interior point c of the domain of f at which f'(c) = 0 or f'(c) does not exist.
cards.n: Every relative extremum occurs at a critical point, but a critical point need not be an extremum — consider x³ at 0.

cards.q: Contrast relative (local) extrema and absolute (global) extrema.
cards.a: A relative extremum is the largest or smallest value on some open interval around the point. An absolute extremum is the largest or smallest value over the entire domain or the entire stated interval.

cards.q: Identify why an endpoint of a closed interval is not counted as a relative extremum.
cards.a: Relative extrema are defined by comparison on an OPEN interval surrounding the point, and an endpoint has no such surrounding interval inside the domain. Endpoints are still candidates for absolute extrema.

cards.q: State the test for intervals on which f is increasing or decreasing.
cards.a: f is increasing on any interval where f'(x) > 0 and decreasing where f'(x) < 0. Locate critical points, build a sign chart for f', and report intervals of x-values.
cards.n: Answer with x-intervals, never y-values, and use the derivative's sign as the justification.

cards.q: Explain how to build a sign chart for f'.
cards.a: Mark every x where f' = 0 or f' is undefined, along with the domain endpoints, on a number line. Test one value inside each resulting subinterval and record only the SIGN of f' there.

cards.q: Describe how to report intervals of increase when f has a hole or a vertical asymptote.
cards.a: Split the number line at every point where f is undefined as well as at every critical point, and never write an interval that runs across a discontinuity.

cards.q: State the First Derivative Test.
cards.a: At a critical point c: if f' changes from positive to negative at c, then f has a relative maximum at c; if f' changes from negative to positive, a relative minimum; if f' does not change sign, neither.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a relative maximum on the AP exam.
cards.a: 'f has a relative maximum at x = c because f'(c) = 0 and f' changes from positive to negative at x = c.' The sign CHANGE of f' must be named, not merely that f'(c) = 0.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a relative minimum.
cards.a: 'f has a relative minimum at x = c because f' changes from negative to positive at x = c.' Alternatively cite f'(c) = 0 together with f''(c) > 0 by the Second Derivative Test.

cards.q: Explain the Candidates Test for absolute extrema on a closed interval.
cards.a: List every critical point in [a, b] together with both endpoints, evaluate f at each candidate, and compare those VALUES. The largest is the absolute maximum and the smallest the absolute minimum.
cards.n: It works because the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees the extrema exist; continuity on [a, b] is the entry ticket.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies an absolute maximum on a closed interval.
cards.a: 'f is continuous on [a, b], and f(c) is the greatest of the values of f at the critical points and the endpoints, so f(c) is the absolute maximum.' Show the table of candidate values.

cards.q: Describe how to justify an absolute extremum on an open or unbounded interval.
cards.a: The Candidates Test does not apply, so argue from the sign of f' across the whole interval: if f' > 0 to the left of c and f' < 0 to the right, then f(c) is the absolute maximum on that interval.
cards.n: This is the required approach whenever the domain is open, infinite, or has no endpoints to test.

cards.q: Define concave up and concave down in terms of f' and f''.
cards.a: Concave up means f' is increasing, equivalently f'' > 0. Concave down means f' is decreasing, equivalently f'' < 0.
cards.n: Concavity describes bending, not rising or falling; a function can decrease while concave up.

cards.q: Define a point of inflection.
cards.a: A point on the graph where f is continuous and the concavity CHANGES, that is, where f'' changes sign.
cards.n: f''(c) = 0 by itself is not enough; the sign of f'' must actually change at c.

cards.q: Explain the wording that justifies a point of inflection.
cards.a: 'f has a point of inflection at x = c because f'' changes sign at x = c', equivalently because f' changes from increasing to decreasing there. Naming the sign change is required.

cards.q: Identify why f''(c) = 0 does not guarantee a point of inflection at c.
cards.a: For $f(x) = x^{4}$, $f''(x) = 12 x^{2}$ is zero at 0 but nonnegative on both sides, so concavity never changes and there is no inflection point. Always test the sign of f'' on each side.

cards.q: State the Second Derivative Test.
cards.a: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) < 0, then f has a relative maximum at c. If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then f has a relative minimum at c. If f''(c) = 0 the test is inconclusive.
cards.n: When the test is inconclusive, fall back on the First Derivative Test with a sign chart.

cards.q: Decide when the Second Derivative Test is the better tool than the First Derivative Test.
cards.a: Use it when f'' is easy to compute and only one critical point needs classifying. Prefer the First Derivative Test when f'' is messy, when f''(c) = 0, or when you already have a sign chart for f'.

cards.q: Describe the checklist for sketching y = f(x) from its formula.
cards.a: Domain; intercepts; asymptotes and end behavior; a sign chart of f' for increasing/decreasing and relative extrema; a sign chart of f'' for concavity and inflection points; then plot key points and connect smoothly.

cards.q: Explain what a relative maximum of f' tells you about the graph of f.
cards.a: It is where f'' changes from positive to negative, so f has a point of inflection there; if f' is positive there, it is also where f is increasing most steeply. It is NOT a maximum of f.
cards.n: Confusing a maximum of f' with a maximum of f is one of the most common graph-reading errors.

cards.q: Identify what the x-intercepts of the graph of f' tell you about f.
cards.a: There f has a horizontal tangent and a possible relative extremum: a maximum if f' crosses from positive to negative, a minimum if from negative to positive. If f' touches zero without crossing, f has neither.

cards.q: Identify what an interval where f' is increasing tells you about f.
cards.a: f' increasing means f'' > 0, so f is concave up on that interval. Where f' is decreasing, f'' < 0 and f is concave down.

cards.q: Explain how to read the concavity of f directly from a graph of f''.
cards.a: f is concave up where the graph of f'' lies above the x-axis, concave down where it lies below, and has points of inflection where f'' crosses the axis.

cards.q: Contrast the statements 'f is decreasing' and 'f prime is decreasing'.
cards.a: f decreasing means f' < 0 and the graph falls. f' decreasing means f'' < 0 and the graph is concave down. A function can fall while concave up, or rise while concave down.

cards.q: Predict the shape of f on an interval where f' < 0 and f'' > 0.
cards.a: f is decreasing and concave up there: it falls but flattens out, so it is decreasing at a slowing rate.

cards.q: Explain the standard optimization procedure.
cards.a: Name variables and draw. Write the quantity to optimize as a function of ONE variable using the constraint. State the domain. Find critical points. Justify the extremum with a derivative test or the Candidates Test. Answer the question actually asked.

cards.q: Explain the points most often lost on an optimization free-response question.
cards.a: Failing to JUSTIFY that the critical point produces the required extremum, and reporting the wrong quantity — giving the x-value when the question asked for the maximum area.

cards.q: Describe how to choose the domain in an optimization problem.
cards.a: Use the physical restrictions: lengths and quantities must be nonnegative, and the constraint caps the largest possible value. A closed domain lets you finish cleanly with the Candidates Test.

cards.q: Explain how to locate horizontal tangent lines on an implicitly defined curve.
cards.a: Set the numerator of the solved $\frac{dy}{dx}$ equal to 0, solve that together with the original equation so the points actually lie on the curve, and check that the denominator is nonzero there.

cards.q: Explain how to determine the concavity of an implicit relation at a given point.
cards.a: Differentiate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ again with respect to x, substitute the expression already found for $\frac{dy}{dx}$, then evaluate at the point. Positive means concave up, negative means concave down.

cards.q: Describe how to show that a point on an implicit curve is a relative minimum.
cards.a: Verify the point lies on the curve, show $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ there, then show $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} > 0$ at that point, and cite the Second Derivative Test by name.

cards.q: Describe the procedure for finding the intervals of concavity of f.
cards.a: Compute f'', find every x where f'' = 0 or f'' is undefined, build a sign chart across the domain of f, and report the x-intervals where f'' > 0 (concave up) and where f'' < 0 (concave down).

cards.q: Describe how to find the critical points of a function whose derivative is a fraction or contains a radical.
cards.a: Simplify f' into a single fraction. Setting the numerator to 0 gives the points where f' = 0; setting the denominator to 0 gives the points where f' is undefined. Keep only values that lie in the domain of f.
cards.n: Points where f' is undefined are critical points too, and they are the ones students most often forget to list.

cards.q: Describe the setup for maximizing the area of a rectangle with a fixed perimeter P.
cards.a: With sides x and y, the constraint 2x + 2y = P gives y = P/2 - x, so A(x) = x(P/2 - x) on 0 < x < P/2. Then A'(x) = P/2 - 2x = 0 at x = P/4, and A''(x) = -2 < 0 confirms a maximum: the square.

cards.q: Explain what a definite integral of a rate of change represents.
cards.a: It gives the NET CHANGE in the accumulated quantity over the interval, not the final amount: $\int_{a}^{b} R(t)\,dt$ is how much the quantity changed from t = a to t = b.
cards.n: Free-response rate problems almost always open with this interpretation.

cards.q: Given F(a) and a rate F', write the expression for F(b).
cards.a: $F(b) = F(a) + \int_{a}^{b} F'(t)\,dt$ — starting value plus accumulated change.
cards.n: Leaving off the initial value F(a) is the single most common accumulation error.

cards.q: Define a Riemann sum for f on [a, b].
cards.a: A sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_{i}^{*}) \Delta x_{i}$ where [a, b] is cut into n subintervals, $x_{i}^{*}$ is a sample point in the i-th subinterval, and $\Delta x_{i}$ is its width.

cards.q: State the subinterval width for n equal subintervals on [a, b].
cards.a: $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$.

cards.q: Write the left Riemann sum for f on [a, b] with n equal subintervals.
cards.a: $L_{n} = \Delta x \left( f(x_{0}) + f(x_{1}) + ... + f(x_{n-1}) \right)$ with $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$; it uses every point EXCEPT the right endpoint b.

cards.q: Write the right Riemann sum for f on [a, b] with n equal subintervals.
cards.a: $R_{n} = \Delta x \left( f(x_{1}) + f(x_{2}) + ... + f(x_{n}) \right)$ with $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$; it uses every point EXCEPT the left endpoint a.

cards.q: Write the midpoint Riemann sum for f on [a, b] with n equal subintervals.
cards.a: $M_{n} = \Delta x \left( f(m_{1}) + f(m_{2}) + ... + f(m_{n}) \right)$ where each $m_{i}$ is the midpoint of its subinterval.
cards.n: With a table of data you can only use midpoints if the table gives the midpoint values.

cards.q: State the trapezoidal sum for f on [a, b] with n equal subintervals.
cards.a: $T_{n} = \frac{\Delta x}{2} \left( f(x_{0}) + 2f(x_{1}) + 2f(x_{2}) + ... + 2f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_{n}) \right)$ — interior values doubled, endpoints not.
cards.n: For unequal widths, add trapezoids one at a time: $\frac{1}{2}(b_{1}+b_{2}) \cdot$ width.

cards.q: Explain how to build a trapezoidal approximation from a table with UNEQUAL subinterval widths.
cards.a: Add the trapezoids individually: for each interval, $\frac{f(x_{i}) + f(x_{i+1})}{2} \cdot (x_{i+1} - x_{i})$, then sum. The 1-2-2-1 shortcut only works for equal widths.
cards.n: AP tables are usually unequally spaced on purpose.

cards.q: Predict whether a LEFT Riemann sum over- or underestimates when f is increasing.
cards.a: Underestimate. On an increasing function the left endpoint is the lowest value on each subinterval.
cards.n: Increasing: left under, right over. Decreasing: reverse.

cards.q: Predict whether a RIGHT Riemann sum over- or underestimates when f is increasing.
cards.a: Overestimate. On an increasing function the right endpoint is the highest value on each subinterval.

cards.q: Predict whether left and right Riemann sums over- or underestimate when f is DECREASING.
cards.a: Left sum overestimates; right sum underestimates. On a decreasing function the left endpoint is the largest value on each subinterval.

cards.q: Predict whether a trapezoidal sum over- or underestimates when f is concave UP.
cards.a: Overestimate. The chord joining two points on a concave-up curve lies above the curve.
cards.n: Trapezoid depends on CONCAVITY, not on increasing/decreasing. Justify with f'' > 0.

cards.q: Predict whether a trapezoidal sum over- or underestimates when f is concave DOWN.
cards.a: Underestimate. The chord lies below a concave-down curve.

cards.q: Predict whether a MIDPOINT sum over- or underestimates by concavity.
cards.a: Concave up: underestimate. Concave down: overestimate — the opposite of the trapezoidal sum.
cards.n: Midpoint and trapezoid always bracket the true value when concavity is constant.

cards.q: State the definite integral as the limit of a Riemann sum.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_{i}) \Delta x$, where $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_{i} = a + i\Delta x$.
cards.n: This is the definition; MC items ask you to convert a limit of a sum into an integral.

cards.q: Translate $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{3}{n}\left(1 + \frac{3i}{n}\right)^{2}$ into a definite integral.
cards.a: $\int_{1}^{4} x^{2}\,dx$. Read $\Delta x = \frac{3}{n}$ so b - a = 3, and $x_{i} = 1 + \frac{3i}{n}$ so a = 1, b = 4.
cards.n: Identify a from the constant inside and b - a from the coefficient of $\frac{1}{n}$.

cards.q: Define an accumulation function.
cards.a: $F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$: a function of its upper limit that accumulates signed area under f from the fixed point a to x. Note F(a) = 0.
cards.n: The dummy variable inside must differ from the limit variable.

cards.q: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1, precisely.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b] and $F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$ for x in [a, b], then F is differentiable on (a, b) and F'(x) = f(x).
cards.n: The continuity hypothesis is required for full credit when the question says 'justify'.

cards.q: State $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{a}^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt$.
cards.a: $f\left(g(x)\right) \cdot g'(x)$ — FTC combined with the chain rule.
cards.n: Forgetting the g'(x) factor is the classic slip.

cards.q: State $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{h(x)}^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt$ when BOTH limits vary.
cards.a: $f\left(g(x)\right)g'(x) - f\left(h(x)\right)h'(x)$ — upper limit term minus lower limit term.

cards.q: State $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{x}^{b} f(t)\,dt$ when the VARIABLE is the lower limit.
cards.a: −f(x). Flip the limits first: $\int_{x}^{b} f = -\int_{b}^{x} f$.
cards.n: The sign flip is worth watching for on MC.

cards.q: Explain how to find where $F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$ is increasing or decreasing.
cards.a: F' = f, so F increases where f > 0 (graph above the axis) and decreases where f < 0. Use the SIGN of f, not whether f is rising.
cards.n: Students routinely confuse 'f increasing' with 'F increasing'.

cards.q: Explain how to find the concavity and inflection points of $F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$ from a graph of f.
cards.a: F'' = f', so F is concave up where f is increasing and concave down where f is decreasing; F has an inflection point where f changes from increasing to decreasing or vice versa.

cards.q: Identify how to locate an absolute maximum of $F(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt$ on a closed interval.
cards.a: Find x where f changes sign from + to - (candidates), include the endpoints, then compare F values computed as accumulated signed areas. Largest wins.
cards.n: Show the actual area arithmetic; a sign chart alone will not earn the absolute-extremum point.

cards.q: State the value of $\int_{a}^{a} f(x)\,dx$.
cards.a: 0 — zero width means zero accumulation.

cards.q: State the effect of swapping the limits of integration.
cards.a: $\int_{b}^{a} f(x)\,dx = -\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$.

cards.q: State the additivity property of definite integrals over adjacent intervals.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{c} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx + \int_{b}^{c} f(x)\,dx$ for any b, even if b lies outside [a, c].
cards.n: Used constantly to fill in missing table values.

cards.q: State the constant multiple and sum rules for definite integrals.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} k f(x)\,dx = k\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ and $\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) \pm g(x) \right)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f\,dx \pm \int_{a}^{b} g\,dx$.
cards.n: There is NO product or quotient rule for integrals.

cards.q: Explain how to express TOTAL area between a curve and the x-axis using an integral.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} |f(x)|\,dx$: split at the zeros of f and negate the pieces where f < 0. The plain integral gives signed area, which is smaller.
cards.n: 'Area' means total area; 'value of the integral' means signed area. Read the wording.

cards.q: State the comparison property for definite integrals.
cards.a: If $f(x) \le g(x)$ on [a, b], then $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx \le \int_{a}^{b} g(x)\,dx$. Also, if $m \le f(x) \le M$, then $m(b-a) \le \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx \le M(b-a)$.

cards.q: State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2 (the evaluation theorem), precisely.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F is any antiderivative of f on [a, b], then $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$.
cards.n: Equivalently $\int_{a}^{b} f'(x)\,dx = f(b) - f(a)$, the Net Change Theorem.

cards.q: State the power rule for antiderivatives.
cards.a: $\int x^{n}\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$ for $n \ne -1$.

cards.q: State $\int \frac{1}{x}\,dx$.
cards.a: $\ln|x| + C$. The absolute value is required.
cards.n: This is the n = -1 exception to the power rule.

cards.q: State $\int e^{x}\,dx$ and $\int e^{kx}\,dx$.
cards.a: $\int e^{x}\,dx = e^{x} + C$ and $\int e^{kx}\,dx = \frac{1}{k}e^{kx} + C$.

cards.q: State $\int a^{x}\,dx$ for a > 0, $a \ne 1$.
cards.a: $\frac{a^{x}}{\ln a} + C$.
cards.n: Dividing by ln a, not multiplying, is the piece people forget.

cards.q: State $\int \sin x\,dx$ and $\int \cos x\,dx$.
cards.a: $\int \sin x\,dx = -\cos x + C$ and $\int \cos x\,dx = \sin x + C$.
cards.n: The minus sign migrates to sine when integrating (opposite of differentiating).

cards.q: State $\int \sec^{2} x\,dx$ and $\int \csc^{2} x\,dx$.
cards.a: $\int \sec^{2} x\,dx = \tan x + C$ and $\int \csc^{2} x\,dx = -\cot x + C$.
cards.n: Every 'co-' function picks up a minus sign.

cards.q: State $\int \sec x \tan x\,dx$ and $\int \csc x \cot x\,dx$.
cards.a: $\int \sec x \tan x\,dx = \sec x + C$ and $\int \csc x \cot x\,dx = -\csc x + C$.

cards.q: State $\int \tan x\,dx$.
cards.a: $-\ln|\cos x| + C$, equivalently $\ln|\sec x| + C$.
cards.n: Comes from u-substitution with u = cos x.

cards.q: State $\int \cot x\,dx$.
cards.a: $\ln|\sin x| + C$.

cards.q: State $\int \sec x\,dx$.
cards.a: $\ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C$.
cards.n: Memorize; the derivation multiplies by $\frac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}$.

cards.q: State $\int \csc x\,dx$.
cards.a: $-\ln|\csc x + \cot x| + C$.

cards.q: State $\int \frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$.
cards.a: $\arctan x + C$.
cards.n: Recognizing this pattern after completing the square is a standard BC move.

cards.q: State $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx$.
cards.a: $\arcsin x + C$.

cards.q: State the general forms $\int \frac{1}{a^{2}+x^{2}}\,dx$ and $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}\,dx$.
cards.a: $\int \frac{1}{a^{2}+x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C$ and $\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}\,dx = \arcsin\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C$.
cards.n: The $\frac{1}{a}$ appears only in the arctan form.

cards.q: Explain the u-substitution procedure for an indefinite integral.
cards.a: Choose u = inner function, compute du = u'(x) dx, replace so the integrand is entirely in u with no x left, integrate in u, then substitute back to x and add C.
cards.n: If any x survives after substituting, the choice of u was wrong.

cards.q: Identify a good choice of u in a substitution.
cards.a: Pick the inside of a composition, the quantity under a radical, an exponent, the argument of a log or trig function, or a denominator — provided its derivative appears (up to a constant) as a factor.

cards.q: Explain how to handle the bounds when using u-substitution on a DEFINITE integral.
cards.a: Either convert them: $\int_{a}^{b} f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)\,du$; or back-substitute to x before plugging in the original bounds. Never mix the two.
cards.n: Plugging original x-bounds into a u-expression is a top-three integration error.

cards.q: Evaluate $\int_{0}^{2} 2x\,e^{x^{2}}\,dx$ using substitution with converted bounds.
cards.a: Let $u = x^{2}$, du = 2x dx; bounds go from 0 to 4. $\int_{0}^{4} e^{u}\,du = e^{4} - 1$.
cards.n: Notice how the bounds change from 0, 2 to 0, 4.

cards.q: Explain when and how to use long division before integrating a rational function.
cards.a: When the numerator's degree is greater than or equal to the denominator's, divide first to get polynomial plus proper remainder, then integrate term by term.
cards.n: Example: $\frac{x^{2}}{x+1} = x - 1 + \frac{1}{x+1}$.

cards.q: Explain how completing the square helps integrate $\frac{1}{x^{2}+6x+13}$.
cards.a: Rewrite the denominator as $(x+3)^{2} + 4$, then substitute u = x + 3 to reach the arctan pattern: $\frac{1}{2}\arctan\left(\frac{x+3}{2}\right) + C$.
cards.n: Use it whenever an irreducible quadratic sits in the denominator.

cards.q: State the integration by parts formula.
cards.a: $\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$. Choose u to be the part whose derivative is simpler and dv to be the part you can integrate.

cards.q: State the LIATE priority for choosing u in integration by parts.
cards.a: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential — whichever type appears FIRST in that list becomes u; the rest is dv.
cards.n: LIATE is a heuristic, not a theorem, but it works on nearly every AP item.

cards.q: Evaluate $\int \ln x\,dx$ using integration by parts.
cards.a: Take $u = \ln x$, dv = dx. Then v = x and $du = \frac{1}{x}dx$, giving $x\ln x - \int 1\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$.
cards.n: The trick is that dv = dx; there is no obvious second factor.

cards.q: Explain when tabular integration by parts is worth using.
cards.a: When one factor differentiates to zero in a few steps (a polynomial) and the other integrates easily (e^x, sin, cos). Columns: derivatives of u, antiderivatives of dv, with alternating signs +, -, +, ...
cards.n: Stop the table when the derivative column reaches 0.

cards.q: Explain the trick for $\int e^{x}\sin x\,dx$, where parts seems to loop.
cards.a: Apply parts twice; the original integral reappears. Set the result equal to I and solve algebraically: $I = \frac{e^{x}\left(\sin x - \cos x\right)}{2} + C$.

cards.q: Explain the setup for integrating with linear partial fractions.
cards.a: Factor the denominator into distinct linear factors, write $\frac{N(x)}{(x-r)(x-s)} = \frac{A}{x-r} + \frac{B}{x-s}$, clear denominators and solve for A and B (plugging in x = r and x = s is fastest).
cards.n: BC only requires NON-REPEATED linear factors.

cards.q: Give the antiderivative pattern once partial fractions are done.
cards.a: Each piece integrates to a log: $\int \frac{A}{x-r}\,dx = A\ln|x-r| + C$, so the answer is a sum of logarithms.
cards.n: Combine with log rules only if the answer choices are written that way.

cards.q: State the degree condition that must hold before partial fractions can be applied.
cards.a: The numerator's degree must be strictly LESS than the denominator's. If not, do polynomial long division first.

cards.q: Define an improper integral and name the two ways an integral can be improper.
cards.a: An integral where the standard definition fails: (1) a limit of integration is $\infty$ or $-\infty$; (2) the integrand is unbounded (has a vertical asymptote) at an endpoint or interior point.

cards.q: Explain how to set up $\int_{a}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$ as a limit.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$. The integral converges if that limit exists and is finite; otherwise it diverges.
cards.n: The limit notation must be WRITTEN on the free-response; answering with $\infty$ plugged in loses the point.

cards.q: Explain how to set up an improper integral when f has a vertical asymptote at the endpoint x = b.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{c \to b} \int_{a}^{c} f(x)\,dx$ with c approaching b from inside the interval.

cards.q: Explain what to do when the integrand has an infinite discontinuity in the INTERIOR of [a, b].
cards.a: Split at the bad point and take a separate limit on each piece. The whole integral converges only if BOTH pieces converge.
cards.n: Integrating straight through a vertical asymptote gives a confidently wrong finite answer.

cards.q: State for which p the improper integral $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x^{p}}\,dx$ converges.
cards.a: It converges when p > 1 (to $\frac{1}{p-1}$) and diverges when $p \le 1$.
cards.n: $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges — the boundary case.

cards.q: Give a decision order for choosing an antidifferentiation technique.
cards.a: 1) Basic formula? 2) Algebra first (expand, split the fraction, long division, complete the square)? 3) u-substitution? 4) Integration by parts (product of unlike types)? 5) Partial fractions (factorable rational)?
cards.n: Always test u-substitution before parts — it is cheaper and more often right.

cards.q: Contrast when you would use u-substitution versus integration by parts.
cards.a: Substitution when the integrand contains a function AND (a constant times) its derivative. Parts when it is a product of two unrelated types whose derivative pattern does not appear.

cards.q: Identify the technique for $\int \frac{2x+1}{x^{2}+x+7}\,dx$.
cards.a: u-substitution: the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator, so the answer is $\ln|x^{2}+x+7| + C$.
cards.n: Always check numerator-equals-derivative-of-denominator before anything fancier.

cards.q: Name the four calculator tasks students are expected to perform on the calculator-active AP Calculus sections.
cards.a: (1) Graph a function in an arbitrary window; (2) solve an equation numerically; (3) compute the numerical value of a derivative at a point; (4) compute the numerical value of a definite integral.
cards.n: Anything beyond these four must be supported by work; bare answers from other calculator features earn no credit.

cards.q: Define a differential equation.
cards.a: An equation relating an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives, e.g. $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2xy$. A solution is a FUNCTION, not a number.
cards.h: → definition plus what a solution is

cards.q: Translate 'the rate of change of y is directly proportional to y' into a differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$ for some constant k.
cards.n: 'Proportional to' always introduces an unnamed constant k; do not assume k = 1.

cards.q: Write Newton's Law of Cooling as a differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dT}{dt} = k\left(T - T_{s}\right)$, where $T_{s}$ is the surrounding temperature and k < 0 for cooling.
cards.n: The solution has the form $T = T_{s} + Ce^{kt}$.

cards.q: Explain how to verify that a given function is a solution of a differential equation.
cards.a: Differentiate the candidate, substitute it and its derivative into BOTH sides of the equation, and simplify to show the sides are identical for all x in the domain.
cards.n: Show the substitution explicitly; asserting it works earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast a general solution with a particular solution.
cards.a: A general solution contains the arbitrary constant C and names an entire family of curves. A particular solution uses an initial condition to pin down C, giving one curve.

cards.q: Define a slope field.
cards.a: A grid of short line segments; the segment at (x, y) has slope $\frac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated there. It shows the shape of every solution curve without solving the equation.

cards.q: Give a strategy for matching a slope field to its differential equation.
cards.a: Test special locations: where are segments horizontal (dy/dx = 0)? Do slopes depend only on x (columns identical) or only on y (rows identical)? Check the sign in each quadrant.
cards.n: Rows identical (same slope all along a horizontal row) means dy/dx depends only on y; columns identical means it depends only on x.

cards.q: Explain how to sketch a particular solution curve on a slope field through a given point.
cards.a: Start at the point and draw a smooth curve that stays TANGENT to the segments it passes, following them left and right; do not cross other solution curves and do not leave the given grid.
cards.n: Curves must pass through the marked point and follow, not connect, the segments.

cards.q: Explain how to spot equilibrium solutions from a slope field or a differential equation.
cards.a: Set $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ and solve for constant y values; on the field these appear as full horizontal rows of flat segments. Those constants are equilibrium solutions.

cards.q: State Euler's method update formulas.
cards.a: $x_{n+1} = x_{n} + h$ and $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated at $(x_{n}, y_{n})$; h is the step size.
cards.n: This is repeated local linearization, one tangent-line step at a time.

cards.q: Explain how to choose the step size h in Euler's method.
cards.a: Divide the total change in x by the number of steps: h = (target x minus start x) / (number of steps). h is negative when stepping to the left of the initial point.
cards.n: Backward steps with negative h are a favorite MC twist.

cards.q: Predict whether Euler's method over- or underestimates the true solution.
cards.a: Concave up solution: Euler UNDERestimates (tangent lines lie below). Concave down: Euler OVERestimates. Determine concavity from the sign of $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$.
cards.n: Same logic as tangent-line approximation, applied repeatedly.

cards.q: Explain the effect of decreasing the step size in Euler's method.
cards.a: Smaller h means more steps and less error, since each tangent-line segment departs from the curve for a shorter distance. The approximation approaches the true solution as h approaches 0.

cards.q: Name the most common Euler's method bookkeeping error.
cards.a: Evaluating the slope with the NEW x but the OLD y (or vice versa). The slope for each step must use the point at the START of that step.
cards.n: Keep an x, y, dy/dx, new y table and fill it row by row.

cards.q: Explain the separation of variables procedure.
cards.a: Write $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y)$, move all y terms with dy to one side and all x terms with dx to the other, integrate both sides, put a single +C on the x side, then solve for y.
cards.n: If dy/dx cannot be factored into f(x)g(y), the equation is not separable.

cards.q: State the test for whether a differential equation is separable.
cards.a: It is separable exactly when $\frac{dy}{dx}$ can be written as a PRODUCT f(x)g(y). Sums like $\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$ are not separable.

cards.q: Explain where the constant of integration goes when separating variables.
cards.a: Add a single C to one side only (conventionally the x side) after integrating; two constants would just combine into one.
cards.n: Forgetting C entirely makes the initial condition unusable.

cards.q: Explain how the absolute value from $\int \frac{1}{y}\,dy$ is handled.
cards.a: Integrating gives $\ln|y|$; exponentiating gives $|y| = e^{C}e^{kx}$, and the sign is absorbed into a new constant so $y = Ce^{kx}$ with C allowed to be negative.
cards.n: On AP responses you may go straight to $y = Ce^{kx}$.

cards.q: Explain the correct order of steps when an initial condition is given.
cards.a: Separate and integrate, substitute the initial condition to solve for C IMMEDIATELY, then solve for y. Solving for y first makes the algebra much worse.
cards.n: This is the standard AP free-response sequence.

cards.q: Explain how the initial condition determines the sign when solving $y^{2} = $ something for y.
cards.a: Take the branch whose sign matches the initial y value: if y(0) = -3, keep the negative square root. Solutions cannot jump branches.
cards.n: Choosing the wrong root is a routine lost point.

cards.q: State the domain convention for a particular solution to a differential equation.
cards.a: The domain is the largest interval containing the initial x value on which the solution is defined and differentiable — it stops at any vertical asymptote or endpoint of validity.

cards.q: State the exponential growth and decay model and its solution.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$ has solution $y = y_{0}e^{kt}$, where $y_{0}$ is the initial amount; k > 0 is growth, k < 0 is decay.
cards.n: Separating variables on dy/dt = ky is the standard derivation; know it both ways.

cards.q: Explain how to find the doubling time for exponential growth.
cards.a: Solve $2y_{0} = y_{0}e^{kt}$, giving $t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$. It does not depend on the starting amount.

cards.q: Explain how to find the half-life for exponential decay.
cards.a: Solve $\frac{1}{2}y_{0} = y_{0}e^{kt}$, giving $t = \frac{\ln(0.5)}{k} = -\frac{\ln 2}{k}$, positive because k < 0.

cards.q: Explain what the constant k means in $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$.
cards.a: k is the relative (per-unit) growth rate: $k = \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dt}$, the fractional change per unit time. Its units are 1 over time.

cards.q: State the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dP}{dt} = kP\left(1 - \frac{P}{L}\right)$, where k > 0 and L is the carrying capacity.
cards.n: Also written $\frac{dP}{dt} = kP - \frac{k}{L}P^{2}$.

cards.q: Define carrying capacity in a logistic model.
cards.a: The value L that the population approaches as $t \to \infty$; it is the nonzero equilibrium solution where $\frac{dP}{dt} = 0$.
cards.n: Also the horizontal asymptote of the logistic curve.

cards.q: Identify where a logistic population grows FASTEST.
cards.a: At $P = \frac{L}{2}$, half the carrying capacity. That is where $\frac{dP}{dt}$ is maximized and where the logistic curve has its inflection point.
cards.n: Maximize dP/dt by setting its derivative with respect to P equal to zero.

cards.q: State $\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)$ for a logistic model with 0 < P(0) < L.
cards.a: L, the carrying capacity.
cards.n: True for any positive starting population; if P(0) > L the population decreases to L.

cards.q: Identify the equilibrium solutions of the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: P = 0 and P = L. P = 0 is unstable; P = L is stable (solutions on both sides move toward it).

cards.q: Explain how to read k and L directly from $\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.04P - 0.0002P^{2}$.
cards.a: Factor: $0.04P\left(1 - \frac{0.0002}{0.04}P\right)$, so k = 0.04 and $\frac{1}{L} = \frac{0.0002}{0.04}$, giving L = 200.
cards.n: Shortcut: L is the ratio of the linear coefficient to the quadratic coefficient.

cards.q: Describe the shape of the logistic solution curve for $0 < P(0) < \frac{L}{2}$.
cards.a: S-shaped: increasing throughout, concave up below $P = \frac{L}{2}$, concave down above it, with an inflection at $P = \frac{L}{2}$ and horizontal asymptote P = L.

cards.q: Contrast the long-run behavior of exponential and logistic growth models.
cards.a: Exponential growth increases without bound. Logistic growth slows as P nears L and levels off at the carrying capacity.
cards.n: Logistic behaves like exponential when P is small compared with L.

cards.q: State the general form of the solution to the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: $P(t) = \frac{L}{1 + Ae^{-kt}}$, where A is fixed by the initial condition.
cards.n: BC students are not required to derive it, but recognizing the form is worth easy MC points.

cards.q: Predict the sign of $\frac{dP}{dt}$ for a logistic model when 0 < P < L and when P > L.
cards.a: Positive for 0 < P < L (population grows) and negative for P > L (population falls back toward L).

cards.q: State the AP Calculus rounding convention on the calculator-active sections.
cards.a: Report decimal approximations to at least THREE places after the decimal point, truncated or rounded. Store full precision in the calculator and round only at the very end.
cards.n: Rounding intermediate values is a classic silent point loss on multi-part free-response.

cards.q: State the formula for the average value of f on [a, b].
cards.a: $f_{avg} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$.
cards.n: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{b-a}$ factor is the most common average-value error.

cards.q: Contrast the average VALUE of f with the average RATE OF CHANGE of f on [a, b].
cards.a: Average value is $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ (an integral). Average rate of change is $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ (a difference quotient, i.e. the average value of f').
cards.n: If the given function is a RATE, its average value is still the integral formula.

cards.q: State the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b], there exists c in (a, b) with $f(c) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ — the function attains its average value somewhere.

cards.q: State the Net Change Theorem for position.
cards.a: $s(b) = s(a) + \int_{a}^{b} v(t)\,dt$: final position equals initial position plus displacement.

cards.q: Define displacement over [a, b] and give its integral.
cards.a: The signed net change in position: $\int_{a}^{b} v(t)\,dt$. It can be negative or zero.

cards.q: Define total distance traveled over [a, b] and give its integral.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)|\,dt$ — always nonnegative. By hand, split at the times where v changes sign and add the absolute values of the pieces.
cards.n: On the calculator section you may enter the absolute value directly.

cards.q: Contrast displacement with total distance traveled.
cards.a: Displacement is net signed change, $\int v\,dt$; total distance is $\int |v|\,dt$. They agree only when v never changes sign on the interval.
cards.n: 'How far did it travel' means distance; 'how far from the start' means displacement.

cards.q: Explain how to find the total distance a particle travels when v(t) changes sign at t = c inside [a, b].
cards.a: Compute $\left|\int_{a}^{c} v\,dt\right| + \left|\int_{c}^{b} v\,dt\right|$; equivalently $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)|\,dt$.
cards.n: Find the sign changes first by solving v(t) = 0.

cards.q: Explain how to determine the units of $\int_{a}^{b} R(t)\,dt$.
cards.a: Multiply the units of R by the units of t: if R is gallons per hour and t is hours, the integral is in gallons.
cards.n: Interpretation questions require units plus a context sentence for full credit.

cards.q: Set up the amount remaining at time T when material enters at rate I(t) and leaves at rate O(t), starting from $A_{0}$.
cards.a: $A(T) = A_{0} + \int_{0}^{T} \left( I(t) - O(t) \right)\,dt$.
cards.n: 'In minus out' tank problems appear on nearly every free-response set.

cards.q: Explain how to find when the amount in an in/out rate problem is at a MAXIMUM.
cards.a: Set the net rate I(t) - O(t) = 0, then check that it changes from positive to negative there; compare candidate values including the endpoints.
cards.h: → critical point of the net rate
cards.n: The maximum is where the rate changes sign, not where the rate is largest.

cards.q: State the area between two curves as functions of x.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$, where f is the upper curve on [a, b] and a, b are the x-coordinates of the intersections.
cards.n: Vertical rectangles: height is top minus bottom, width is dx.

cards.q: Explain how to decide which function is 'on top' in an area problem.
cards.a: Test a sample x strictly between the intersection points and compare the two outputs; whichever is greater is the top function on that subinterval.
cards.n: Subtracting in the wrong order gives a negative area — a giveaway that you flipped it.

cards.q: State the area between two curves as functions of y.
cards.a: $\int_{c}^{d} \left( f(y) - g(y) \right)\,dy$, where f is the RIGHT curve and g is the LEFT curve, and c, d are the y-coordinates of the intersections.
cards.n: Horizontal rectangles: length is right minus left, thickness is dy.

cards.q: State when integrating with respect to y is easier for an area problem.
cards.a: When the region's left and right boundaries are single curves but the top or bottom boundary switches, or when the curves are naturally written as x = f(y).
cards.n: Choosing dy can turn three integrals into one.

cards.q: Name the setup trap involving dx versus dy.
cards.a: Mixing them: using x-bounds with a dy integral, or leaving a function of x inside a dy integral. Everything inside the integral must be in the same variable as the differential.
cards.n: Check the bounds: dx bounds are x-values, dy bounds are y-values.

cards.q: Explain how to find the area of a region whose boundary curves intersect at MORE than two points.
cards.a: Find all intersections, split the interval at each one, determine which function is on top on each piece with a test point, and add the separate integrals (each written top minus bottom).
cards.n: A single integral with absolute value also works on the calculator section.

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$ can understate the AREA when the curves cross inside [a, b].
cards.a: Past the crossing the integrand turns negative, so that piece cancels part of the earlier piece. Area needs $\int_{a}^{b} |f(x) - g(x)|\,dx$.

cards.q: State the general volume formula for a solid with known cross sections.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} A(x)\,dx$, where A(x) is the area of the cross section at x. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis integrate with dx; perpendicular to the y-axis, dy.

cards.q: Give the volume integral when cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are SQUARES with base in the region between f and g.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$ — the side length is the vertical distance between the curves.
cards.n: No $\pi$ appears; cross-section solids are not solids of revolution.

cards.q: Give the volume integral when cross sections are RECTANGLES of height twice the base.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} 2\left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$: area = base times height = s times 2s.
cards.n: Read the stated height ratio carefully; it varies problem to problem.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of an EQUILATERAL TRIANGLE with side s, and the resulting volume integral.
cards.a: $A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^{2}$, so $V = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of a SEMICIRCLE whose DIAMETER is s, and the resulting volume integral.
cards.a: $A = \frac{\pi}{8}s^{2}$ (radius is $\frac{s}{2}$), so $V = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$.
cards.n: Check whether the problem gives the diameter or the radius; using s as the radius multiplies the answer by 4.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of an ISOSCELES RIGHT TRIANGLE with the LEG on the base, versus the HYPOTENUSE on the base.
cards.a: Leg on the base: $A = \frac{1}{2}s^{2}$. Hypotenuse on the base: $A = \frac{1}{4}s^{2}$.
cards.n: The wording 'leg' versus 'hypotenuse' changes the answer by a factor of 2.

cards.q: State the disc method for revolving a region about the x-axis.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( R(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$, where R(x) is the distance from the axis to the curve. Use it when the region touches the axis of revolution.
cards.h: → pi times integral of radius squared

cards.q: State the disc method for revolving about the y-axis.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{c}^{d} \left( R(y) \right)^{2}\,dy$, with the curve solved for x in terms of y and the bounds as y-values.

cards.q: Explain how to write the radius when revolving about a horizontal line y = c instead of the x-axis.
cards.a: The radius is the distance from the line to the curve: R(x) = |f(x) − c|. Above the line use f(x) - c; below it use c - f(x).
cards.n: Subtracting the axis value is the whole trick; the rest of the setup is unchanged.

cards.q: Explain how to write the radius when revolving about a vertical line x = k.
cards.a: R(y) = |x(y) − k|, the horizontal distance from the line to the curve, and integrate with respect to y.

cards.q: State the washer method.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( \left( R(x) \right)^{2} - \left( r(x) \right)^{2} \right)\,dx$, where R is the outer radius and r the inner radius. Use it when a gap separates the region from the axis.
cards.h: → pi times integral of R squared minus r squared

cards.q: Name the algebra trap in the washer method.
cards.a: Writing $\left( R - r \right)^{2}$ instead of $R^{2} - r^{2}$. You subtract the AREAS of the two circles, not the radii.
cards.n: This error is worth several points and is easy to miss in a rush.

cards.q: Explain how to set up a washer volume about a horizontal line y = c below the region.
cards.a: Outer radius R = (far curve) - c and inner radius r = (near curve) - c, then $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( R^{2} - r^{2} \right)\,dx$. Identify which curve is farther from the axis, not which is on top.
cards.n: When the axis lies above the region, the roles of the curves swap.

cards.q: State the shell (cylindrical shells) method for revolving about the y-axis.
cards.a: $V = 2\pi\int_{a}^{b} x \cdot \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$ — radius times height times thickness. About a vertical line x = k, the radius becomes |x - k|.
cards.h: → two-pi times integral of radius times height
cards.n: Shells are NOT required by the AP CED; discs and washers suffice, but shells can be faster.

cards.q: State when the shell method is more convenient than washers.
cards.a: When the region is easy to describe in x but is revolved about a VERTICAL axis (or vice versa), so shells avoid solving the curves for the other variable.

cards.q: State the arc length formula for y = f(x) on [a, b].
cards.a: $L = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left( f'(x) \right)^{2}}\,dx$, valid when f' is continuous on [a, b].
cards.n: BC only; on the exam this is almost always evaluated with the calculator.

cards.q: State the arc length formula for a curve written as x = g(y) on [c, d].
